common_name: Lady Vansittart Camellia (Variegated White-and-Pink Striped Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Lady Vansittart is a long-cultivated antique Camellia japonica notable for the striking, unpredictable white-and-pink striping of its blooms.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Lady Vansittart is a historic Camellia japonica cultivar dating to the 1800s, prized for its semi-double flowers striped and marbled in white and rose-pink in an irregular, ever-varying pattern from bloom to bloom, occasionally producing solid pink or solid white flowers on the same plant, a trait long fascinating to camellia collectors. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter and early spring flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mine-no-Yuki has a wide, spreading, almost groundcover-like habit that sets it apart from the more upright sasanqua cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Mine-no-Yuki, whose name translates roughly to 'snow on the peak,' is a classic sasanqua camellia grown for its wide, spreading, low-mounding habit and its abundant, large, white, semi-double to double flowers produced in a heavy fall flush, offering both a groundcover-scale alternative to upright sasanquas and reliable late-season color when little else is blooming. Its sprawling form makes it useful for espalier, bank plantings, or training against a wall as well as an informal low hedge. Setsugekka and other sasanquas tolerate more sun than japonicas, and Mine-no-Yuki follows that pattern, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Prune only lightly to shape after flowering, since flower buds set later in the growing season.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Shishi-Gashira is a compact, dwarf sasanqua camellia widely used as a low foundation shrub or informal hedge.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Shishi-Gashira is one of the most widely planted dwarf sasanqua camellias, valued for its compact, dense, mounding habit that stays low without regular pruning, making it a popular foundation shrub, low hedge, or mass planting in Gulf South landscapes. It produces abundant, deep rose-pink, semi-double flowers in a heavy fall flush, offering reliable color when few other shrubs are blooming, and like other sasanquas it tolerates more direct sun than Camellia japonica cultivars, blooming well in partial shade to full sun. Its naturally tidy, slow-growing form means it rarely needs shearing to maintain shape, and pruning, if wanted, should be done lightly right after flowering.

common_name: Pink Ruffles Azalea (Ruffled Pink Southern Indica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Ruffles is a Southern Indica azalea grown for its heavily ruffled, wavy-edged pink petals, distinct from the flatter blooms of most other Southern Indica cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Pink Ruffles is a Southern Indica azalea distinguished from most other cultivars in the group by its heavily ruffled, wavy-margined petals, giving the bright pink spring flowers extra texture and dimension against the large, evergreen shrub's dense foliage. Like other Southern Indica cultivars it produces its heaviest bloom in a single spectacular spring flush and provides substantial year-round structure the rest of the year. Water deeply during establishment and dry spells, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Glacier is a compact Kurume azalea bred for a dense, heavily flowered, pure white spring display.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Glacier is a compact Kurume-type azalea producing a dense, heavy flush of small, pure white, hose-in-hose flowers each spring, its tidy mounding habit and fine-textured evergreen foliage making it well suited to foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings where a smaller-scale white azalea is wanted. Its full, floriferous bloom and manageable size have kept it a mainstay in Southern gardens alongside other classic Kurume selections. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Higasa is a Satsuki-type azalea that blooms later in the season than most Southern Indica and Kurume cultivars, and is a popular subject for bonsai as well as landscape use.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Higasa is a Satsuki-type azalea prized for its unusually large, deep rose-pink flowers with a darker blotch, blooming later in late spring to early summer after most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas have finished, which extends the overall azalea bloom season in the landscape. Satsuki azaleas like Higasa are also widely used in bonsai for their fine branching and responsiveness to training, though it performs equally well as an unpruned landscape shrub. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the current season's flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
